title: Executive Order 14110: Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
authors: The White House (Executive Office of the President, Joseph R. Biden Jr.)
access: open official text
verification: FULL TEXT read at origin (Federal Register HTML) 2026-11-05: Sections 1-12 including the dual-use foundation-model reporting thresholds (models trained with >10^26 operations; computing clusters >10^20 ops/s), NIST guidelines tasks, HHS AI Task Force and safety-programme directives, OMB Chief-AI-Officer guidance, and the national-security-memorandum directive.
relevance: The Biden administration's whole-of-government AI order: eight guiding principles and binding agency tasks on safety evaluations, dual-use model reporting under the Defense Production Act, critical-infrastructure risk assessment, CBRN screening, watermarking standards work, competition (CHIPS, small business), worker support, civil rights, consumer/patient protection, privacy, federal AI use and talent. It operated until revoked by EO 14179 (Jan 2025); its thresholds and programmes shaped reporting practice and international commitments. Reading note: text of the order only — implementing reports (NIST guidelines, OMB memos) are separate documents.

title: Executive Order 14179: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence
authors: The White House (Executive Office of the President)
access: open official text; Federal Register site bot-gated (FR API and govinfo copy used)
verification: Full text read at govinfo.gov 2026-11-05; bibliographic fields cross-checked against the Federal Register API (title, EO number 14179, signing date 2025-01-23, publication 2025-01-31).
relevance: The order that reversed course from EO 14110: it revokes the 2023 order, directs agencies to suspend or rescind actions under it (including revising OMB memos M-24-10 and M-24-18 within 60 days), and states a policy 'to sustain and enhance America's global AI dominance in order to promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security', with an AI action plan due in 180 days. Reading note: the pair of orders (14110/14179) is the clearest single demonstration that national AI governance is politically volatile — same statute base, opposite directives two administrations apart.

title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
access: open page + free PDF
verification: Framework landing page read at origin 2026-11-05 (version 1.0, release date, four functions, purpose, companions); the 60-page framework PDF itself not opened this session. Page notes AI RMF 1.0 is being revised under the AI Action Plan.
relevance: The most-used voluntary AI risk framework: four core functions — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — meant to help organisations incorporate trustworthiness into how AI systems are designed, developed, used and evaluated. Voluntary by design, so it shapes practice through procurement references and alignment (e.g., referenced in OMB memos) rather than binding duties. Useful for the standards topic as the counterpart to the EU's binding act and ISO/IEC 42001's certifiable management system.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act) — official policy overview
authors: European Commission
date: in force 2024-08-01; prohibitions 2025-02-02; GPAI rules 2025-08-02; generally applicable 2026-08-02 (with Omnibus exceptions)
access: open page
verification: Official Commission policy page read at origin 2026-11-05 (regulation name/number, entry-into-force and application dates, four risk tiers, Omnibus exceptions). The consolidated legal text itself not read this session; specific-article claims must await a text read.
relevance: The first comprehensive AI law: a single regulation sorting AI systems into unacceptable (banned), high-risk (pre-market obligations), transparency (chatbot/deepfake disclosure) and minimal-risk tiers, plus separate layered duties for general-purpose AI models. Its staggered application schedule and the 2026 'AI Omnibus' adjustments make timing claims easy to get wrong — the dates above are from the Commission's own page. Read together with Hoch & Muegge (influence limits) and the standards-brief records already in the catalogue.

title: National AI Strategy 2.0 — AI for the Public Good, for Singapore and the World
authors: Smart Nation Singapore / National AI Council
access: open page; strategy PDF at file.go.gov.sg/nais2023.pdf
verification: Official Smart Nation strategy page read at origin 2026-11-05: NAIS 2.0 vision, the May 2026 Update with 10 refreshed priorities under the National AI Council (chaired by PM Lawrence Wong), 70+ company AI Centres of Excellence, a $150 million Enterprise Compute Initiative, AI Verify and Project Moonshot, and international cooperation lines. Full PDF not read this session.
relevance: A small state's whole-of-nation AI play: industry adoption programmes, government upskilling, sovereign evaluation tooling (AI Verify; Moonshot evals), and explicit international alignment. Useful contrast to large-economy strategies because implementation detail (funding lines, evaluation tooling) is unusually concrete. The 2026 Update shows strategies as living documents, not one-off launches.

title: 生成式人工智能服务管理暂行办法 / Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
authors: Cyberspace Administration of China + six agencies (NDRC, MOE, MOST, MIIT, MPS, NRTA)
access: open translation (China Law Translate); Chinese original on cac.gov.cn
verification: FULL TRANSLATION read at origin 2026-11-05: provider obligations — prohibited-content duties, non-discrimination, IP/personal-rights respect, lawful training-data handling, producer responsibility, labelling per deep-synthesis rules, complaint handling, and security assessment + algorithm filing for services with 'public opinion properties or the capacity for social mobilization'. Original Chinese text not read; translation is community-maintained and widely cited.
relevance: The world's first binding generative-AI-specific regulation, effective August 2023 — before the EU AI Act entered into force. It obliges providers of public-facing services to prevent prohibited and discriminatory content, label synthetic images/video, protect user data, and undergo security assessment and algorithm filing when services have public-opinion or mobilisation capacity. Comparing its content-control framing with the EU's risk-tier framing is one of the cleanest cross-regime contrasts available.

title: 人工智能生成合成内容标识办法 / Measures for Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content
authors: Cyberspace Administration of China, MIIT, Ministry of Public Security, National Radio and Television Administration
access: open translation (China Law Translate); pairs with mandatory national standard GB 45438-2025
verification: FULL TRANSLATION read at origin 2026-11-05: explicit visible labels on AI-generated text/audio/images/video/virtual scenes preserved in exports; implicit metadata labels recording provider name/code and content reference number; duties on distribution platforms to verify, alert and prevent label removal/falsification. Effective 1 Sep 2025 alongside GB 45438-2025. Unofficial community translation; Chinese original not read.
relevance: The most detailed synthetic-content labelling regime in force anywhere: it operationalises what the EU AI Act only sketches in its transparency article, covering both visible marks and embedded metadata across the whole content lifecycle, with platform-side verification duties. Directly relevant to watermarking/provenance research (SynthID-Text, C2PA) already in the catalogue: this is the demand side of those techniques.

title: Making AI Less "Thirsty": Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models
authors: Pengfei Li, Jianyi Yang, Mohammad A. Islam, Shaolei Ren
access: open arXiv page
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read.
relevance: The paper that made AI's water use a mainstream policy question: it gives a method to estimate the on-site and off-site water footprint of AI training and inference, distinguishing direct evaporation from indirect (electricity) water use. Headline figures: training GPT-3 in Microsoft's US data centres can directly evaporate ~700,000 litres of freshwater, and global AI demand may drive 4.2-6.6 billion cubic metres of water withdrawal in 2027. Authors' projections depend on adoption and efficiency assumptions; operational water data from operators remains scarce (the same gap ISIS Malaysia documents).

It grounds the chips-and-geopolitics topic upstream of fabs: export controls on gallium/germanium (MOFCOM record in catalogue) sit in the same material chain. title: Queued Up: 2026 Edition — Characteristics of Power Plants Seeking Transmission Interconnection as of the End of 2025
authors: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Electricity Markets and Policy division (with GridTracker)
institution: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, US Department of Energy
access: open page + open PDF
verification: Report landing page read at origin 2026-11-05 with exact figures: ~8,200 active projects seeking interconnection totalling ~2,060 GW (1,312 GW generation + 749 GW storage) at end-2025 (10% below prior year); median request-to-operation duration exceeded 5 years for 2025-built projects; of 2000-2020 requesters only 13% reached commercial operation by end-2025 (75% withdrawn). Full PDF not read.
relevance: The canonical evidence that US grid interconnection queues are the binding constraint behind the AI-buildout story: over 2 TW waiting, five-plus-year waits, and only ~13% historical completion. Explains why data-centre developers chase 'in-front-of-the-meter' deals (the AirTrunk/PLN-type PPAs in the catalogue) and why connection-queue governance appears in the grid topic. Scope is US queues; other markets differ.

title: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale
authors: Guilherme Penedo, Hynek Kydlicek, Loubna Ben allal, Anton Lozhkov, Margaret Mitchell, Colin Raffel, Leandro Von Werra, Thomas Wolf (Hugging Face)
access: open arXiv page; datasets on Hugging Face
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read.
relevance: The most-used open web-scale pretraining corpus: 15T tokens from 96 Common Crawl snapshots plus a 1.3T-token education-filtered subset (FineWeb-Edu) whose models show 'dramatically better performance on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks like MMLU and ARC'. Its fully documented filtering ablations are the public evidence that data curation choices — dedup, filtering — move benchmark outcomes, supporting the how/data topic's curation-dependence claim with reproducible methods.

title: The Data Provenance Initiative: A Large Scale Audit of Dataset Licensing & Attribution in AI
authors: Shayne Longpre, Robert Mahari, Anthony Chen et al. (MIT/Media Lab collaboration)
access: open arXiv page; explorer at dataprovenance.org
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read.
relevance: A 1,800+-dataset audit tracing provenance, creators and licence conditions: over 70% of popular hosting-site datasets omit licence information and over 50% are miscategorised — described by the authors as 'a crisis in misattribution and informed use'. This quantifies the copyright/data-governance uncertainty behind every training-data claim in the catalogue, and documents that closed datasets dominate lower-resource languages (connects to SEA-LION/IndicTrans2's open-data rationale).

title: Airavata: Introducing Hindi Instruction-tuned LLM

title: Measuring digital development: Facts and Figures 2026
authors: International Telecommunication Union (ITU-D)

verification: Report landing page read at origin 2026-11-05 (2026 edition, November 2026 aggregates): ~6.3bn people online (~76% of world population) with 2bn offline; internet use 93% in high-income vs 32% in low-income countries; mobile-ownership/internet-use gap narrowing. Gives the infrastructure/connectivity topic an official, regularly-updated denominator and a reminder that offline populations are the hard boundary of 'AI for everyone' claims.

title: MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering
authors: Jun Shern Chan, Neil Chowdhury, Oliver Jaffe, James Aung, Dane Sherburn, Evan Mays, Giulio Starace, Kevin Liu, Leon Maksin, Tejal Patwardhan, Lilian Weng, Aleksander Madry (OpenAI)

Its 16.9% bronze-rate is a concrete calibration point for both capability claims and the automation-anxiety debates in the jobs topic.
